```{r setup}
library(robotstxtr)
```

## Two axes, selected explicitly

`allowed_by_robots_text()` and `allowed_by_robots_url()` always use Google's
matcher. Multi-engine integrations should use the parallel, versioned facade
instead, `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` and `robots_evaluate_url_v1()`, which
make every caller select both axes explicitly:

- `robots_policy_ruleset`: how fetch evidence (a missing file, a server error,
  a redirect) becomes a policy action, per engine.
- `matcher_backend`: which matcher evaluates the rules.

The `robots_product_token` selects the robots user-agent group only; it is
never sent as an HTTP header. Everything below runs offline.

```{r}
robots <- "user-agent: *
disallow: /private
allow: /private/public
"

x <- robots_evaluate_text_v1(
  robots,
  "https://example.com/private/report",
  robots_product_token = "Googlebot",
  robots_policy_ruleset = "google",
  matcher_backend = "google"
)
x
```

The result keeps neutral fetch evidence, engine policy, matcher availability,
and the final URL decision in separate columns:

```{r}
x$results[c(
  "evidence_status", "policy_status", "matcher_availability",
  "matcher_status", "url_decision", "reason"
)]
```

## Explicit non-decisions

An unavailable matcher returns `capability_unavailable` rather than silently
falling back to Google. The RFC 9309 backend is such a matcher:

```{r}
robots_evaluate_text_v1(
  robots,
  "https://example.com/private/report",
  robots_product_token = "mybot",
  robots_policy_ruleset = "assumed_rfc9309",
  matcher_backend = "rfc9309"
)$results[c("matcher_status", "reason", "url_decision")]
```

## Bounded vendor profiles

The Google backend accepts any valid product token and returns Google
semantics for it, which is not a claim about the crawler that token names. The
Yandex and Bing backends are bounded to their supported profiles and never
generalize to other tokens:

```{r}
contract <- robots_engine_contract_v1()
contract$matcher_availability
contract$matcher_capability$yandex$supported_profiles[
  c("profile_id", "accepted_token", "profile_revision")
]
contract$matcher_capability$bing$supported_profiles[
  c("profile_id", "accepted_token", "profile_revision")
]
```

Any other token on those backends is a checked non-decision, not a decision:

```{r}
robots_evaluate_text_v1(
  robots,
  "https://example.com/private/report",
  robots_product_token = "YandexImages",
  robots_policy_ruleset = "yandex",
  matcher_backend = "yandex"
)$results[c("matcher_status", "reason", "url_decision")]
```

The Yandex and Bing backends are independent, unofficial compatibility
profiles and make no production-crawler parity claim.

## Contract metadata

`robots_engine_contract_v1()` publishes the schema revision, policy and
matcher revisions, and capability metadata; `robots_engine_contract_v2()`
adds the extended matcher-status set that the Bing backend uses.

```{r}
contract$contract_id
contract$schema_revision
robots_engine_contract_v2()$matcher_status_set
```

`as_legacy_robots_decisions_v1()` converts a v1 result evaluated with the
Google policy and the Google matcher to the `robots_decisions` shape the
headline functions return. The v1 contract is specified in the
[engine-aware contract design document](https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr/-/blob/main/design/engine-contract-v1.md),
and the Bing backend and the v2 status set in the
[Bing integration v2 specification](https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr/-/blob/main/design/robotstxtbing-integration-v2-spec.md).
